1.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is the reason:]

Isaiah is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

As the Hebrew prophets did on many occasions, in this chapter Isaiah emphasizes a point by using words together that have very similar sounds. The words translated as “supply” and “support” differ in just one letter. It is often difficult to reproduce this kind of word play in another language, but if your language does have similar terms that you can use in this instance, as the ULT does, it would be appropriate to do that in your translation. If not, you could show the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [all support]

Isaiah says **all supply of bread and all supply of water** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [the entire supply of bread and water]

Isaiah uses a repetitive series of clauses from here to the end of verse 3 to communicate that what he is saying should be understood as comprehensive and overwhelming. Use a form in your language that someone would use to describe a situation that is comprehensive and overwhelming.

2.q: גִּבּ֖וֹר וְ⁠אִ֣ישׁ מִלְחָמָ֑ה שׁוֹפֵ֥ט וְ⁠נָבִ֖יא וְ⁠קֹסֵ֥ם וְ⁠זָקֵֽן
2.note: This is a list of categories of people that others depend on. Since they do not refer to particular individuals, they can all be translated with plural nouns as in the UST. Alternate translation: [the mighty men and the warriors and the judges and the prophets and the ones who practice divination and the elders]
This is a person who claims that he can tell the future by looking at things like animal parts and leaves. See how you translated similar words in Isaiah 2:6.

3.note: The expression **the one instructed of enchantment** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the one who knows enchantments]

Isaiah is using **one lifted up of face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a dignitary” or “an honored person.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and an honored person]

4.note: This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh, as the UST does.

The word translated as **capriciousness** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. Some interpreters have noted that a slight change in the consonants would result in the word “children,” which seems like a closer parallel with the term **youths**. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [and children]

5.note: The expression **the people will be oppressed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And people will oppress one another]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [each person by another person and each person by their neighbor]

Isaiah is referring to all of society by naming two major components, **the youth** and **the elderly**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [People of every age will act insolently against one another]

Isaiah is using the adjective **elderly** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [old people]

Isaiah is using the adjectives **despised** and **honored** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [and people who are despised against people who are honored]

6.note: Here the masculine terms **man** and **brother** have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [someone will grab a relative]
This is the beginning of what the man said to **his brother** If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote with a quote margin, as modeled by the UST.
Here, **hand** represents “authority.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [under your authority]

The man is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and take care of this ruin that is under your authority]

7.note: See the discussion of the term **saying** in the Introduction to 1 Samuel. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

Isaiah is using **he will lift up** as a common expression of the culture to mean “rise up in protest.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will respond] or [he will cry out]

8.note: Isaiah is speaking of **Jerusalem** and **Judah** as if they were living things that could stumble and fall. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Jerusalem have failed and the people of Judah have been ruined]
Here, **tongue** represents “speech” or “what they say.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [what they say]

8.q: כִּֽי־לְשׁוֹנָ֤⁠ם וּ⁠מַֽעַלְלֵי⁠הֶם֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֔ה לַ⁠מְר֖וֹת עֵנֵ֥י כְבוֹדֽ⁠וֹ
8.note: Here, **to** marks **defy the eyes of his glory** as the goal or purpose of their words and deeds being against Yahweh. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [because their tongue and their deeds are against Yahweh so that they defy the eyes of his glory]

Here, **the eyes of his glory** represents the “radiance of his glory.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the radiance of his glory]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [brilliant light]

9.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **Sodom** was openly sinful and shameless, so are the people of Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as the people of Sodom were openly sinful and unashamed]

Isaiah is using the phrase **Woe to their soul** to express a strong feeling of grief and warning about the judgment coming upon them. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what made Isaiah grieve. Alternate translation: [Disaster is coming upon them]

10.note: Isaiah is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are righteous]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if the consequences of righteous deeds were **fruit** that could be eaten. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the results of their deeds will be good for them]

11.note: Isaiah is using the phrase **Woe to the wicked** to express a strong feeling of grief and warning about the judgment coming upon them. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what made Isaiah grieve. Alternate translation: [Disaster is coming upon the wicked]

Isaiah is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **recompense**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he has done to others]

Here, **his hands** represents “his actions” or “what he has done.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his deeds]

The expression **will be done to him** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [will come upon him]

12.q: עַמִּ⁠י֙ נֹגְשָׂ֣י⁠ו מְעוֹלֵ֔ל וְ⁠נָשִׁ֖ים מָ֣שְׁלוּ ב֑⁠וֹ
12.note: The pronouns **its** and **it** refer to Yahweh’s people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [My people, the oppressors of my people are a child, and women rule over my people]

Isaiah actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their rulers are as incompetent as children, and those who should not be in authority are controlling them]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if wrong moral influence were physically **leading** people **astray** on a path. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones who guide you are causing you to sin]

Here Isaiah is speaking of how the people live as if it were a **way** or **path** that they walked along. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they confuse you about how you should live]

13.note: Here Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh’s judgment were a legal proceeding in which he had **stationed himself** to prosecute and was **standing** to render a verdict. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [taken his place to argue his case and is positioned to judge]

14.q: יְהוָה֙ בְּ⁠מִשְׁפָּ֣ט יָב֔וֹא עִם־זִקְנֵ֥י עַמּ֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠שָׂרָ֑י⁠ו
14.note: This is the beginning of what Yahweh said to the leaders. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh, as modeled by the UST.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **judgment**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will begin judging]

Isaiah is repeating forms of the pronoun **you** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [And you, their leaders, have consumed]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his people were the **vineyard** that the leaders had **consumed**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have stripped my people of everything they had]

15.q: מ⁠ל⁠כם תְּדַכְּא֣וּ עַמִּ֔⁠י וּ⁠פְנֵ֥י עֲנִיִּ֖ים תִּטְחָ֑נוּ
15.note: Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the leaders for oppressing his people. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You must not crush my people and grind the faces of the poor!]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the oppressors of his people were physically **crushing** them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you cruelly mistreat my people]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the oppressors of the poor were **grinding** their **faces**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you humiliate them the poor]

Yahweh is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are poor]

The phrase **the declaration of the Lord, Yahweh of Armies** closes a direct quotation by identifying the speaker. In your translation, use a natural way of attributing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [thus declares the Lord Yahweh of Armies]

16.note: Here, **neck outstretched** represents “arrogance.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in an arrogant way]

Isaiah assumes that readers will know the social significance of **walking and mincing, and they tinkle with their feet**. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [this is how they would walk to attract men, possibly because the bracelets on their ankles were connected by chains decorated with bells so they could not take normal steps]

17.note: The term translated as **so** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [therefore the Lord will make scabby]

18.note: Isaiah is using the term **day** to mean “time,” since time consists of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [At that time]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **anklets** that are characterized by **splendor**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the splendid anklets]

The **anklets** are a kind of jewelry worn around the ankles that jingles when the wearer walks. If your readers would not be familiar with what anklets are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [ankle bracelets]

The **headbands** are decorative bands worn on the head. If your readers would not be familiar with what headbands are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and the head ornaments]

Crescents are a kind of ornamental jewelry shaped like a crescent moon. If your readers would not be familiar with what crescents are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [crescent-shaped ornaments]

20.note: The **headdresses** are ornamental head coverings. If your readers would not be familiar with what headdresses are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the decorative head coverings]

Ankle chains are a kind of decorative chain worn around the ankles. These chains connected the two ankles so that women had to walk with short, mincing steps. If your readers would not be familiar with what ankle chains are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [decorative chains worn on the ankles]

21.note: The **signet rings** are rings engraved with a seal used to stamp official documents. If your readers would not be familiar with what signet rings are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [rings used as official seals]

22.note: The **capes** are outer wrapping garments. If your readers would not be familiar with what capes are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [outer wraps]

The **cloaks** are large covering garments. If your readers would not be familiar with what cloaks are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [outer garments]

23.note: Mirrors in this context are pieces of polished metal used to see one’s reflection. If your readers would not be familiar with what these mirrors are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [reflective surfaces]

The **turbans** are head coverings made by wrapping cloth around the head. If your readers would not be familiar with what turbans are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [their head wrappings]

24.q: תַ֨חַת בֹּ֜שֶׂם מַ֣ק יִֽהְיֶ֗ה וְ⁠תַ֨חַת חֲגוֹרָ֤ה נִקְפָּה֙ וְ⁠תַ֨חַת מַעֲשֶׂ֤ה מִקְשֶׁה֙ קָרְחָ֔ה וְ⁠תַ֥חַת פְּתִיגִ֖יל מַחֲגֹ֣רֶת שָׂ֑ק כִּי־תַ֖חַת יֹֽפִי׃
24.note: Isaiah uses a repetitive series of clauses in this verse to communicate that what he is saying should be understood as comprehensive and overwhelming. Use a form in your language that someone would use to describe a situation that is comprehensive and overwhelming. Alternate translation: [Instead of all their beauty and finery, they will have only filth and ruin]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and instead of a belt, there will be a rope]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and instead of the craft of hairdo, there will be baldness]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and instead of a robe, there will be girding of sackcloth]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they will be branded instead of being beautiful]

25.note: Here, **the sword** represents “warfare” or “battle.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [will fall in warfare]

Here, **your might** represents “your mighty warriors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your strong warriors]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and your strong warriors will fall in battle]

26.note: Isaiah is speaking of Jerusalem’s **gates** as if they were living things that could **lament and mourn**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the people at her gates will lament and mourn]

The expression **she will be emptied** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [her enemies will empty her]

Isaiah is speaking of Jerusalem as if **she** were a woman who could be **emptied** of her possessions and **sit on the ground** in grief. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Jerusalem will be stripped of her wealth; her people will sit on the ground in mourning]
